name: Static vs Dynamic Control
display_title: Hold when you can, move when you need to
description: Learn when to settle a pin and when to change position as frames appear. Practice staying connected through transitions without turning every escape into a scramble.
summary: Top control combines settling a useful pin with changing grips or position when the opponent’s escape makes that pin difficult to keep.
overview: Even a settled pin needs small adjustments. Movement is useful when it preserves an advantage or creates a new one; circling for its own sake can give the bottom player the space they need.
key_takeaways: Settle when your base and controls prevent the opponent from making useful space.
Move when a grip change, hip switch, or new pin answers the escape better than squeezing the old hold.
Keep a connection during transitions so the opponent cannot turn freely underneath you.
Re-establish balance and control after moving; reaching mount is not the same as holding it.
Choose from the position you see rather than assigning static or mobile styles by body size.

bjj_applications.scenario: You have side control and the bottom player cannot recover an inside frame
bjj_applications.application: Maintain a stable base and adjust to their bridge without unnecessarily opening a gap. Work toward your next attack from that control.
bjj_applications.outcome: You use the pin you earned instead of giving it away through needless movement.

bjj_applications.scenario: Strong inside frames start lifting your torso away
bjj_applications.application: Change your grip, hip angle, or pin while tracking their hips. Do not insist on driving straight into frames that are now supporting your weight.
bjj_applications.outcome: You answer the new structure before a knee returns inside.

bjj_applications.scenario: You move from side control toward mount and feel a leg being trapped
bjj_applications.application: Check your balance and clear the leg only if you can do so under control. If half guard is established, treat it as another passing problem rather than claiming a finished mount.
bjj_applications.outcome: You recognize the position you actually landed in.

common_mistakes.mistake: Holding tighter after the useful controls are gone
common_mistakes.consequence: You spend effort on a grip that no longer prevents the escape.
common_mistakes.correction: Identify what changed and choose a new control that addresses it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Moving to the next pin before controlling the current transition
common_mistakes.consequence: The bottom player turns into the gap or gets their knees back inside.
common_mistakes.correction: Maintain contact with the hips or upper body and settle before changing again.

training_exercises.name: Follow one escape
training_exercises.description: Start in side control. Bottom uses a controlled bridge and hip escape; top may adjust the pin or move to another pin. Reset on guard recovery, reversal, a stable new pin, or a tap.
training_exercises.focus: Change only as much as the escape requires.

training_exercises.name: Arrive and settle
training_exercises.description: Start beside the legs after a pass, with neither player fully settled. Top tries to establish side control or mount while bottom recovers guard. Reset when either position is clearly established.
training_exercises.focus: Make control after movement part of the transition.

knowledge_assessment.question: Is constant movement evidence of good dynamic control?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Only if it preserves an advantage. If the opponent gains space, turns freely, or recovers guard, the movement did not maintain control.
